Summary:
The abstract describes a large-scale empirical study that systematizes more than 50 low- and high-level implementation choices in on-policy reinforcement-learning (RL) algorithms. By training 250 000 agents across five continuous-control environments, the authors quantify how those choices influence performance and offer practical recommendations.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[82]

Inference strategy justification:
Only the abstract was provided, so I reconstructed the full reasoning chain that logically links the stated problem (undocumented design choices) to the study’s empirical evidence and to two natural, safety-relevant interventions (adopting the recommended choices and using the open framework for reproducible benchmarking). Moderate inference (confidence 2-3) was applied where the abstract implies but does not spell out details (e.g., names of section headings, exact recommendations).

Extraction completeness explanation:
All core causal-interventional paths present in the abstract are captured: two top-level risks (“performance unreliability” and “research progress slowdown”) flow through problem analysis, theoretical insight, design rationale, implementation mechanism, and validation evidence, and finally motivate two actionable interventions. All nodes participate in at least one edge, and no intervention is connected directly to a risk.

Key limitations:
• Only information in the abstract is available, so node descriptions and confidence scores rely on inference rather than full-paper details.
• Specific recommended hyper-parameters are not listed, so the intervention node is necessarily generic.
• Section titles are approximated (“Abstract”) because the source text does not provide them.
